figure-248.summary: Italian composer of the Violin Concerto No. 2 with its “La Campanella,” rumored to have sold his soul to the devil.
facts: He would nick his strings so they snapped mid-performance, then finish the piece on the strings that were left.
The last of his “24 Caprices” was reworked into sets of variations by Franz Liszt, Johannes Brahms, and Sergei Rachmaninoff.

figure-249.summary: Italian opera composer who wrote “The Barber of Seville” in less than three weeks.
facts: He gave up opera at 37, and his name lives on in the beef tenderloin dish tournedos Rossini.
His “William Tell” Overture is still used as background music for racing scenes.

figure-250.summary: Italian composer who brought the love stories of ordinary people to the stage in “Madama Butterfly” and “La Bohème.”
facts: “Nessun dorma” (“None shall sleep”) from “Turandot” was the theme of the BBC's coverage of the 1990 World Cup.
He died before finishing “Turandot,” and the composer Franco Alfano completed it.

figure-251.summary: French painter who loved depicting ballerinas' weary poses in rehearsal rooms and backstage, as in “The Dance Class.”
facts: He dressed his wax sculpture “Little Dancer Aged Fourteen” in a real tutu and ribbon.
Unlike his fellow painters, he preferred interiors and artificial light to the outdoors.

figure-252.summary: French Impressionist who captured people dancing in the sunlight in warm colors, as in “Bal du moulin de la Galette.”
facts: He started out at 13 painting designs on dishes at a porcelain factory.
Even after his hands stiffened, he kept painting with brushes his assistants placed in his grip.

figure-253.summary: French painter who scandalized Paris with “Luncheon on the Grass,” shown at the Salon des Refusés.
facts: He was condemned for painting a nude woman of his own day rather than a figure from mythology.
Young Impressionists looked up to him, yet he never once exhibited at an Impressionist show.

figure-254.summary: French painter who quit stockbroking for Tahiti and left vividly colored works like “Tahitian Women.”
facts: He spent nine weeks with Vincent van Gogh in Arles before a bitter quarrel drove them apart.
The hero of W. Somerset Maugham's novel “The Moon and Sixpence” is modeled on his life.

figure-255.summary: French painter who founded pointillism, placing tiny dots of unmixed color so they blend in the viewer's eye.
facts: He spent two years on a single painting, “A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte.”
He died at 31 of an illness whose cause remains unclear.

figure-256.summary: Norwegian painter of “The Scream,” in which a figure clutches its face beneath a blood-red sky.
facts: Losing his mother and older sister as a child left a mark on his art for the rest of his life.
“The Scream” exists in four versions, two of which were stolen and later recovered.

figure-257.summary: American dancer known as the mother of modern dance, who cast off pointe shoes and corsets to dance barefoot.
facts: She drew her movements from the poses of ancient Greek sculpture.
In 1927 in Nice, she was killed when the long shawl around her neck caught in the wheel of a car.

figure-258.summary: German physicist, trained as a doctor, who formulated the conservation of energy in its general form.
facts: In 1851 he invented the ophthalmoscope for looking inside the eye and became famous overnight.
He also studied how the ear perceives sound and music.

figure-259.summary: German mathematician whose geometry of curved space laid the mathematical groundwork for relativity ahead of time.
facts: Sixty years later, Albert Einstein adopted that mathematics as it stood.
His conjecture on the distribution of prime numbers is still unsolved, with a $1 million prize on offer.

figure-260.summary: German mathematician who founded set theory and proved that infinity comes in more than one size.
facts: In 1891 he used the diagonal argument to show that there are more real numbers than natural numbers.
Under attack from his opponents, he suffered repeated bouts of depression and died in a sanatorium.

figure-261.summary: French mathematician who showed that the motion of three mutually attracting celestial bodies cannot be solved with a single formula.
facts: This insight became the starting point of chaos theory.
The topology conjecture he left behind was solved about 100 years later, in 2003, by Grigori Perelman.

figure-262.summary: Italian chemist who formulated the law that equal volumes of gas at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules.
facts: His name lives on in Avogadro's number, the number of particles in one mole, familiar from high-school chemistry.
Ignored in his lifetime, his idea was accepted only in 1860, four years after his death.

figure-263.summary: German physician who discovered the bacteria behind tuberculosis and cholera, cementing the idea that germs cause disease.
facts: He developed methods for growing one type of bacterium at a time on solid media such as potato slices and gelatin.
World Tuberculosis Day, March 24, marks the day in 1882 when he announced his discovery of the tuberculosis bacterium.

figure-264.summary: French physiologist who showed that the body keeps its internal environment stable even as the outside world changes.
facts: In 1926 the American physiologist Walter Cannon gave this idea the name “homeostasis.”
He was also the first to show that the liver produces sugar.

figure-265.summary: British missionary and explorer who became the first European to cross south-central Africa on foot from the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean.
facts: The first European to see a vast waterfall there, he named it Victoria Falls after the queen.
After all contact with him was lost, he was found at Ujiji in 1871 by the journalist Henry Morton Stanley.

figure-266.summary: American inventor, originally a painter, who created a telegraph system that sent letters using only dots and dashes.
facts: His name lives on in Morse code, in which the distress signal SOS is three dots, three dashes, three dots.
The first telegraph message was “What hath God wrought.”

figure-267.summary: British-born inventor who sent the human voice over wires and received a telephone patent in 1876.
facts: The “bel” in decibel, the unit of loudness, comes from his name.
His mother and his wife were both deaf, and he devoted his life to teaching speech.

figure-268.summary: British engineer who, in 1825, ran a steam locomotive carrying passengers and freight on the first public railway.
facts: He learned to read at 18 and taught himself by working on machines in the coal mines.
The 1,435 mm track gauge he chose became the world's standard gauge, which South Korea's railways also use.

figure-269.summary: British physicist from a brewing family who measured how work turns into heat with an experiment in which falling weights churned water.
facts: The joule (J), the SI unit of energy, is named after him.
Legend has it that even on his honeymoon, he and Lord Kelvin tried to measure the difference in water temperature between the top and bottom of a waterfall.

figure-270.summary: British physicist who devised an absolute temperature scale independent of any substance and calculated its zero to be about −273°C.
facts: He was knighted for helping lay the transatlantic undersea telegraph cable.
The kelvin, the unit behind lighting color temperatures such as 6500K, comes from the noble title he received.

figure-271.summary: French physicist who described in equations the forces by which two current-carrying wires attract and repel each other.
facts: The “A” in the 2A printed on a phone charger stands for the ampere, the unit of electric current named after him.
He named his field “electrodynamics” and also coined the word “solenoid.”

figure-272.summary: German physicist who discovered that electric current is proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance.
facts: He made the discovery while working as a high-school teacher, but the academic world's cold reception even led him to quit teaching.
The unit of resistance, the ohm, bears his name and is written with the Greek letter Ω.

figure-273.summary: British mathematician called the father of the computer for designing the Analytical Engine, driven by punched cards.
facts: Short of money and technology, he never finished them in his lifetime.
In 1991, London's Science Museum built a Difference Engine to his design, and it calculated correctly to 31 digits.

figure-274.summary: French entomologist who, from 1879, published the ten volumes of “Souvenirs entomologiques,” vividly recording insects' lives and habits.
facts: He uncovered the habits of dung beetles and hunting wasps through observation alone.
Instead of pinning specimens, he studied insects by watching them alive in the fields.

figure-275.summary: French historian who rewrote his nation's history with the common people, not kings, as its protagonists.
facts: He was the first historian to popularize “Renaissance” as the name of an era.
In his “History of France,” he portrayed Joan of Arc as a hero of the people and made her widely known.

figure-276.summary: American inventor who in 1839 mixed rubber with sulfur and heated it, making it able to withstand both heat and cold.
facts: He reportedly found the key after accidentally dropping sulfur-laced rubber onto a hot stove.
The Goodyear tire company was founded 38 years after his death and simply borrowed his name.

figure-277.summary: American inventor who made elevators trustworthy by adding a safety device that stops the car even if the rope snaps.
facts: At an exhibition, he rode the platform himself and had the rope cut to demonstrate it.
The company he founded, Otis, is now the world's largest elevator maker.

figure-278.summary: American activist who led the National American Woman Suffrage Association and fought for women's right to vote for over 50 years.
facts: After voting in the 1872 presidential election, she was arrested and fined $100, which she never paid.
In 1979 she became the first real woman to appear on a U.S. one-dollar coin.

figure-279.summary: American activist who escaped slavery and campaigned for abolition through speeches and his newspaper “The North Star.”
facts: His autobiography became a bestseller and exposed the reality of slavery.
He met Abraham Lincoln to press for fair treatment of Black soldiers.

figure-280.summary: American activist whose 1851 speech at the women's rights convention in Akron, Ohio, gave voice to Black women.
facts: Born into slavery, she sued a white man and won back her son, who had been sold away.
Her famous line “Ain't I a Woman?” appears only in a version published 12 years later.

figure-281.summary: Joseon religious leader from an impoverished yangban family who founded Donghak in Gyeongju in 1860, teaching people to serve Haneullim, the Lord of Heaven.
facts: Because it made no distinction of class or gender, farmers flocked to it.
He was executed in Daegu on charges of deluding the people and disturbing the social order.

figure-282.summary: Late-Joseon statesman who ruled for ten years in place of his son Gojong, rebuilding Gyeongbokgung and closing all but 47 Confucian academies.
facts: The dangbaekjeon coins he minted to pay for the palace work sent prices soaring and stirred public resentment.
After the 1871 U.S. expedition to Korea (Sinmiyangyo), he erected anti-foreign steles nationwide and closed the country's doors.

figure-283.summary: Joseon reformist politician who led the 1884 Gapsin Coup, which collapsed after just three days.
facts: He put forward a 14-point reform plan to abolish aristocratic privilege and overhaul the tax system.
After ten years wandering in Japan, he was shot dead by Hong Jong-u in Shanghai in 1894.

figure-284.summary: Korean journalist who in 1896 launched “The Independent,” Korea's first privately run newspaper, in Hangul and English editions.
facts: After taking part in the Gapsin Coup, he went to the United States and became the first Korean to earn a medical degree.
He founded the Independence Club and built Independence Gate, and the paper's launch date, April 7, became Korea's Newspaper Day.

figure-285.summary: Minister of the Korean Empire who left a farewell letter and took his own life when the Eulsa Treaty was signed.
facts: He traveled around the world on a trip to attend the Russian tsar's coronation.
Chungjeong-ro, a street in Seoul, is named after his posthumous title, Chungjeonggong.

figure-286.summary: New Zealand physicist whose gold foil experiment revealed a tiny, dense nucleus at the center of the atom.
facts: In a 1936 lecture, he recalled that it was “as if you fired a shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.”
A physicist who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, he now appears on New Zealand's $100 banknote.

figure-287.summary: Austrian physicist who devised the equation that describes, as a wave, where an electron is likely to be found.
facts: His thought experiment of a cat in a box was proposed in 1935 to poke fun at an interpretation of quantum mechanics.
His book “What Is Life?” influenced Watson and Crick, who uncovered the structure of DNA.

figure-288.summary: Italian physicist who in 1942 started up the first man-made nuclear reactor beneath the stands of a University of Chicago stadium.
facts: Rough back-of-the-envelope estimates such as “How many piano tuners are there in Chicago?” are called Fermi estimates.
In 1938, while traveling to accept his Nobel Prize, he fled with his family to the United States.

figure-289.summary: American physicist who directed a secret laboratory in the desert and built the first atomic bomb.
facts: Christopher Nolan's 2023 film “Oppenheimer” told his life story and won the Academy Award for Best Picture.
After opposing the hydrogen bomb, he was stripped of his security clearance in 1954, a decision that was reversed only in 2022.

figure-290.summary: Austrian physicist who gave the theoretical explanation of a nucleus splitting in two, yet was left out of the Nobel Prize.
facts: After fleeing the Nazis to Sweden in 1938, she and her nephew Otto Frisch gave the process the name “nuclear fission.”
Element 109, meitnerium, is named after her.

figure-291.summary: American chemist who explained how atoms bond using quantum mechanics in “The Nature of the Chemical Bond.”
facts: He is the only person to have won both the Nobel Prize in Chemistry and the Nobel Peace Prize without sharing either one.
In 1970 he published a book urging large doses of vitamin C to ward off colds, putting him at odds with the scientific community.

figure-292.summary: Austrian psychoanalyst who, in “The Interpretation of Dreams,” probed the deep layers of the mind hidden even from ourselves.
facts: A slip of the tongue that reveals a person's true feelings is still called a “Freudian slip.”
At 82, he fled the Nazis and went into exile in London.

figure-293.summary: Russian physiologist who made dogs salivate at nothing more than a sound played before feeding.
facts: Although his work is usually linked to a bell, his lab records mostly mention a metronome and a buzzer.
He became Russia's first Nobel laureate for his earlier research on digestion.

figure-294.summary: American astronomer who brought the universe into living rooms around the world with the TV documentary series “Cosmos.”
facts: In 1977 he put a golden record carrying the sounds and images of Earth aboard the Voyager spacecraft.
He called the photo of Earth taken from 6 billion kilometers away the “Pale Blue Dot.”

figure-295.summary: American naval officer and computer scientist who made it possible to write programs in English words instead of machine code.
facts: She created FLOW-MATIC, the foundation of the COBOL language.
She popularized the term “bug” by spreading the story of a real moth, stuck in a circuit, that was taped into a logbook.

figure-296.summary: American astronomer whose observations showed that galaxies exist beyond the Milky Way and that the universe is expanding.
facts: The law that more distant galaxies are receding faster is now called the Hubble–Lemaître law.
The space telescope launched in 1990 bears his name.

figure-297.summary: Belgian priest and astronomer who first proposed that the universe began from a single, extremely tiny point.
facts: The name “Big Bang” was coined on the radio in 1949 by Fred Hoyle, who disliked the idea.
Albert Einstein at first told him that his calculations were correct but his physics was abominable.

figure-298.summary: American agricultural scientist who restored the cotton-depleted soil of the South by rotating crops with peanuts and sweet potatoes.
facts: Born into slavery, he taught at Tuskegee Institute for 47 years.
The claim that he invented peanut butter is a popular misconception.

figure-299.summary: Japanese bacteriologist who found the syphilis bacterium in the brains of paralytic patients and died in Africa while studying yellow fever.
facts: His left hand, fused by a burn from a hearth at age two, was restored by surgery when he was about 15, which inspired him to become a doctor.
His portrait was on Japan's 1,000-yen note from 2004 until it was replaced on the new notes in 2024.

figure-300.summary: Japanese physicist who predicted the meson, the particle that binds the particles inside the nucleus together.
facts: In 1949 he became the first Japanese person to win a Nobel Prize.
The particle was discovered 12 years after his prediction, just as he had foreseen.

figure-301.summary: Dutch painter who built canvases from vertical and horizontal lines and the three primary colors alone, as in “Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow.”
facts: He painted trees in ever simpler forms until only lines and planes remained.
In 1965, Yves Saint Laurent transferred that grid directly onto a dress.

figure-302.summary: Russian painter who opened the door to abstract art with unrecognizable images such as his “Composition” series.
facts: The turning point reportedly came when one of his own paintings, hung upside down, struck him as more beautiful.
He felt he could hear a sound in every color and gave his works titles drawn from musical terms.

figure-303.summary: Spanish Surrealist who brought dreamscapes to canvas with the melting clocks of “The Persistence of Memory.”
facts: His upturned mustache followed him everywhere like a trademark.
In 1969 he designed the flower-shaped logo for Chupa Chups lollipops.

figure-304.summary: Dutch printmaker who created the endless staircase of “Ascending and Descending” and the self-drawing “Drawing Hands.”
facts: In “Reptiles,” a lizard crawls out of a patterned sheet of paper and then back into it.
His endless staircase was inspired by an optical illusion devised by the Penroses, father and son.

figure-305.summary: Russian composer of “The Rite of Spring,” whose premiere set off a riot in the audience.
facts: Its meters shift so constantly that even the musicians struggled to count them.
“The Rite of Spring” accompanied the dinosaur sequence in Disney's 1940 film “Fantasia.”

figure-306.summary: French composer of “Clair de lune,” who painted sound with color and atmosphere rather than clear-cut melody.
facts: He was captivated by Javanese gamelan music, which he heard at the 1889 Paris World's Fair.
He himself disliked being labeled an Impressionist.

figure-307.summary: French composer of “Boléro,” which repeats the same melody for 15 minutes while adding more and more instruments.
facts: At the 1984 Winter Olympics, a gold-medal ice dance performed to “Boléro” earned perfect scores.
For a pianist who had lost his right arm, he wrote a concerto for the left hand alone.

figure-308.summary: American composer of “Rhapsody in Blue,” who brought jazz and orchestral music together on one stage.
facts: At 15 he worked for a sheet-music publisher, promoting new songs by playing them on the piano.
He died suddenly of a brain tumor at the age of 38.

figure-309.summary: Finnish composer who, under Russian rule, set the national epic “Kalevala” to music.
facts: “Finlandia” could at one time be performed only under other titles because of censorship.
Around age 60 he stopped composing and fell silent for 30 years; his birthday, December 8, is celebrated as the Day of Finnish Music.

figure-310.summary: Russian pianist and composer of the “Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini” and the Piano Concerto No. 3.
facts: After his First Symphony was savaged by critics, he could not compose for more than three years, until treatment helped him produce his Piano Concerto No. 2.
Fleeing the revolution, he moved to the United States and made his living as a performer.

figure-311.summary: British filmmaker who mocked Hitler in “The Great Dictator” and made the world laugh and cry as the bowler-hatted Tramp.
facts: In “Modern Times,” he created the unforgettable scene of being swallowed up by a giant machine.
Branded a communist, he was denied reentry into the United States in 1952.

figure-312.summary: Czech writer of “The Metamorphosis,” about a man who wakes up one morning transformed into an insect.
facts: Nightmarishly bureaucratic, dead-end situations are called “Kafkaesque” in English.
His work survived only because a friend ignored his dying wish to have his manuscripts burned.

figure-313.summary: British novelist of “Mrs Dalloway,” who set down her characters' thoughts just as they flowed through their minds.
facts: She wrote that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write.
In 1917 she and her husband set up a press in their home and published her books themselves.

figure-314.summary: Best-selling British novelist of all time, who left 66 detective novels and 14 short-story collections.
facts: She created the Belgian detective Hercule Poirot and the elderly village sleuth Miss Marple.
Thanks to her experience working as a pharmacy dispenser, her descriptions of poisons are remarkably accurate.

figure-315.summary: British novelist, a doctor by training, who created the detective of 221B Baker Street.
facts: In 1893 he killed off his hero at a waterfall, then brought him back in 1901 under pressure from readers.
He modeled the detective on the keen observational skills of Joseph Bell, his teacher at Edinburgh's medical school.

figure-316.summary: Japanese novelist of “I Am a Cat,” which satirizes human society through a cat's eyes.
facts: He quit his lectureship at Tokyo Imperial University to become a staff writer for the Asahi Shimbun.
His portrait appeared on Japan's 1,000-yen note introduced in 1984.

figure-317.summary: British prime minister whose speeches rallied the nation in World War II and who even won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
facts: He declared that he had nothing to offer but “blood, toil, tears and sweat.”
His portrait has appeared on the back of the British £5 note issued since 2016.

figure-318.summary: American aviator who in 1932 became the first woman to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic.
facts: In 1937, during an attempt to fly around the world, she vanished over the Pacific.
Her plane has never been found, and in October 2026 a new expedition set out for Nikumaroro Island.

figure-319.summary: American industrialist whose conveyor-belt assembly line made cars affordable for ordinary people.
facts: In 1913 the time to assemble one Model T dropped from 12.5 hours to 93 minutes.
In 1914 he raised the daily wage from $2.34 to $5 to curb high worker turnover.

figure-320.summary: Italian inventor who sent signals across the Atlantic without any wires.
facts: Starting with experiments in the attic of his family home, he went on to win the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics.
The Titanic's distress calls were also sent out on equipment he developed.

figure-321.summary: Chinese revolutionary who became the first provisional president of the Republic of China after more than 2,000 years of imperial rule collapsed.
facts: He championed the Three Principles of the People: nationalism, democracy, and the people's livelihood.
Zhongshan Roads across China and the Zhongshan suit take their name from his alias, Zhongshan.

figure-322.summary: Indian statesman who, as the first prime minister after independence in 1947, laid the nation's foundations over 17 years.
facts: From 1930, he wrote 196 letters from prison to his daughter Indira, which became “Glimpses of World History.”
He led the policy of non-alignment, taking neither side in the Cold War.

figure-323.summary: American sociologist and activist who was the first Black person to earn a PhD from Harvard.
facts: In “The Souls of Black Folk,” he wrote that “the problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color-line.”
He played a leading role in founding the NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People), a Black civil rights organization.

figure-324.summary: Confucian scholar of the Korean Empire who raised a righteous army in his seventies, was taken to Tsushima, and died there for his country.
facts: When the order to cut topknots was issued, he defied it, saying, “You may cut off my head, but never my hair.”
After the Eulsa Treaty, he gathered a righteous army in Taein, North Jeolla Province.

figure-325.summary: Korean independence activist who carried Emperor Gojong's credentials to the 1907 Hague Peace Conference to declare the Eulsa Treaty invalid.
facts: Because of Japanese obstruction, he was barred from entering the conference.
The lodging where he died became a memorial museum, and his remains were returned to his homeland only in 1963.

figure-326.summary: Independence activist of the Korean Patriotic Organization who threw a bomb at Japanese military leaders in Hongkou Park, Shanghai.
facts: He carried out the attack at 23 and was executed that December in Kanazawa, Japan.
The attack prompted the Chinese government to begin supporting the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea.

figure-327.summary: Korean independence activist who helped found the New People's Association and Daeseong School in Pyongyang, insisting the nation be won back by training capable people.
facts: He founded the Young Korean Academy (Heungsadan), and Seoul's Dosan-daero avenue and Dosan Park are named after his pen name, Dosan.
Putting honesty above all else, he urged, “Do not lie, even if it costs you your life.”

figure-328.summary: Korean religious leader who renamed Donghak as Cheondogyo in 1905 and spearheaded preparations for the March 1st Movement.
facts: He headed the 33 national representatives who signed the Declaration of Independence.
Bosung College, taken over in 1910 by the Cheondogyo he led, later became Korea University.

figure-329.summary: Korean Buddhist monk and poet whose 1926 collection “The Silence of Love” sang of parting and longing.
facts: He copied his prison essay “On the Independence of Joseon” onto tissue paper and smuggled it out.
He reportedly built his house, Simujang, facing north so he would not have to look at the Japanese Government-General building.

figure-330.summary: Korean poet of the Japanese colonial period who left behind “Prologue,” which opens, “Until the day I die, let me look up to the sky.”
facts: Arrested while studying in Japan, he died in Fukuoka Prison at the age of 27.
His posthumous collection was published in 1948, and the 2016 film “Dongju” portrayed his life.

figure-331.summary: Korea's first female Western-style painter, who held a solo oil-painting exhibition in Seoul in 1921 and spoke out for women in her “Divorce Confession.”
facts: She serialized a travelogue of her journey through Europe and America in the magazine “Samcheolli.”
After her divorce, amid condemnation and poverty, she died at 52 in 1948 in a hospital ward for people with no next of kin.

figure-332.summary: Korean children's author who popularized “eorini,” a respectful word for children, and founded the Saekdonghoe society to create Children's Day.
facts: He published the magazine “Eorini” (“Children”) and toured the country telling fairy tales aloud.
The first Children's Day was May 1, 1923, and in 1946 it was moved to May 5.

figure-333.summary: Korean independence fighter who led the Northern Military Administration Office's troops to a crushing victory over the Japanese at Cheongsanri in 1920.
facts: At 17 he freed his family's slaves and gave away land to them.
In 1930 in Manchuria, he was shot dead by Park Sang-sil, a member of the Goryeo Communist Youth Association.

figure-334.summary: Former hunter turned Korean independence fighter who lured the Japanese army into the Bongo-dong valley in 1920 and won a major victory.
facts: He led righteous armies with marksmanship honed by hunting, and he was portrayed in the 2019 film “The Battle: Roar to Victory.”
He was forcibly relocated to Central Asia in 1937, and his remains were brought back to Daejeon National Cemetery in 2021.

figure-335.summary: Korean independence activist who led the Independence Club and the Manmin Gongdonghoe (People's Assembly) and trained young people at the YMCA.
facts: In 1927 he was chosen as the first president of the Singanhoe, which united left and right.
His funeral was held as a public “social funeral” that drew crowds of 100,000.

figure-336.summary: Korean educator who poured the fortune he made selling brassware into founding Osan School in Jeongju in 1907.
facts: During the March 1st Movement, he signed as one of the 33 national representatives.
He asked in his will that his body be used to teach students, but the Japanese colonial authorities blocked it.

figure-337.summary: Korean historian who wrote “The Painful History of Korea” in 1915, arguing that even when a nation is lost, its history endures.
facts: In “The Bloody History of the Korean Independence Movement,” he documented the atrocities surrounding the March 1st Movement.
He served as the second president of the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea.

figure-338.summary: Korean politician who founded the New Korea Youth Party, sent a delegate to the Paris Peace Conference and set up the independence preparation committee right after liberation.
facts: While striving to unite left and right, he was assassinated in Hyehwa-dong, Seoul, in 1947.
As president of the Joseon Jungang Ilbo, he bore the consequences when the paper erased the Japanese flag from an athlete's photo.
